name: Bee venom (topical)

lead: Bee venom creams and masks are marketed in Korean skincare as a gentler stand-in for botulinum toxin injections. Brands say they tighten the skin and smooth expression lines.

Honey bee venom is a mix of peptides and enzymes; melittin is about half of the peptides, and the creams are thought to work by a mild tingling or plumping effect on the surface. The sources do not show how a cream would deliver them through skin to relax facial muscle. Wrinkle trials of the topical product were not found; the one controlled human study identified tested an ointment on jaw-muscle tension.

paras: People apply it as a cream, serum or mask in an evening routine, often around the forehead and eyes, and generally judge results over weeks. It is positioned as a non-injection option.
Phospholipase A2 in the venom is a main allergen, and venom can cause local inflammation. Bee-sting allergy is a reason to avoid it. Data on cosmetic-product safety were not found.

angle.text: Topical bee venom is marketed in Korean skincare as a natural 'faux-tox' that tightens skin and smooths expression lines. The venom's peptides are bioactive in the lab, but wrinkle trials of the topical product were not found.

lead: Topical bee venom is honey bee venom, or a purified or synthetic version of it, used in creams and masks marketed in Korean skincare as a natural 'faux-tox' alternative to botulinum toxin injections for wrinkles. Brand claims generally describe it as tightening or smoothing expression lines.

Honey bee venom is a mixture of peptides and enzymes. Melittin makes up roughly half of the venom peptides, phospholipase A2 is a main allergen, and apamin, hyaluronidase and histamine are also present [1].

Published human evidence for wrinkle reduction was not found among the sources reviewed. The one identified controlled human study of bee venom ointment concerned jaw-muscle tension, not appearance [2].
infobox: Topical; also apitherapy by sting or injection

paras: Honey bee venom contains melittin, phospholipase A2, apamin, hyaluronidase and mast cell degranulating peptide, along with small molecules such as histamine [1]. Cosmetic products may use harvested venom or synthetic peptides; the sources reviewed do not document what concentrations commercial products contain.
In K-beauty marketing, bee venom creams are described as producing a 'tightening' effect and an alternative to neurotoxin injections. The sources reviewed contain no trial testing these claims.

Apitherapy practitioners claim bee venom treats conditions such as arthritis and multiple sclerosis; Wikipedia reports that the American Cancer Society states there is no scientific evidence apitherapy treats cancer or other disease, and that clinical trials found it ineffective for multiple sclerosis and potentially worsening symptoms [1].

A randomized, double-blind trial applied bee venom ointment with a three-minute massage over the masseter muscles for 14 days in people with temporomandibular disorders and compared it with a petrolatum placebo, measuring muscle tension [2][3]. It was a muscle-relaxation study rather than a wrinkle study.

Other registered trials use ultrasound-driven delivery (phonophoresis) of bee venom for psoriasis, ulcers, osteoarthritis, sinusitis and post-hernia complications [4][5][6]. None assessed facial wrinkles.
Phospholipase A2 is a main venom allergen and venom can cause local inflammation [1]. Sources reviewed do not report adverse-event rates for cosmetic creams.
